title: Count Equal-Value Index Pairs
statement:
You get an integer array nums. Count the index pairs (i, j) with i < j and nums[i] == nums[j].

The answer can exceed 32 bits but always fits in a 64-bit integer (and safely in a JavaScript number).

examples.why: The three 4s form 3 pairs and the two 7s form 1 pair.
Four equal values give 4·3/2 = 6 pairs, not 3 (each value pairs with every later copy, not only its neighbour).

hints: Checking every pair works but is quadratic. Does the position of equal values matter, or only how many there are?
A value that appears k times forms k·(k − 1)/2 pairs.
In one pass: when you meet a value, it pairs with every earlier copy. Add the number of copies seen so far, then increase that count.

explain.intuition:
Positions only matter to say i < j, and any two copies of a value can be ordered that way exactly once. So the answer depends only on how often each value occurs: k copies make k·(k−1)/2 pairs.

A single pass does the same thing incrementally: the new copy of a value pairs with each copy seen before it, so add the current count and then bump it. Summing 0 + 1 + … + (k−1) gives the same formula.
steps: Keep a map seen from value to how many times it has appeared so far.
For each value x: add seen[x] (0 if new) to the answer, then increase seen[x].
pitfalls: Counting only neighbouring equal values; [1, 2, 1] has a pair.
Counting (i, j) and (j, i) both, or pairing an index with itself.
Storing the answer in a 32-bit integer in a typed language: 100 000 equal values make about 5·10⁹ pairs.

solutions.title: Check every pair
solutions.idea: Two nested loops over i < j.

solutions.title: Running count
solutions.idea: Each new copy pairs with all earlier copies of the same value.

followups: Count pairs where nums[i] == nums[j] and i·j is divisible by k.
